content: The nature of the hepatitis C virus (HCV) and its capacity for rapid mutation appear to hinder the development of an effective neutralizing immune response. This suggests that post-exposure prophylaxis using immune globulin (IG) is unlikely to be effective. Additionally, IG is now produced from plasma that has been screened for anti-HCV antibodies. In an experimental study, IG derived from anti-HCV-negative plasma was administered to chimpanzees one hour after exposure to HCV. The IG failed to prevent infection or disease in these animals. The use of alpha interferon for post-exposure prophylaxis has not been studied. While alpha interferon therapy is considered safe and effective for treating chronic hepatitis C, the mechanisms underlying its efficacy remain poorly understood. Interferon may only be effective in the presence of an established infection. It must be administered via injection and can cause side effects. Based on these considerations, antiviral agents are not recommended for post-exposure prophylaxis of HCV infection. In the absence of effective prophylaxis, individuals exposed to HCV may benefit from knowing their infection status. This allows them to seek evaluation for chronic liver disease and potential treatment. Sustained response rates to alpha interferon therapy are generally low, ranging from 10% to 20% in the United States. Mild to moderate side effects are common, leading to therapy discontinuation in up to 15% of patients. No clinical, demographic, biochemical, serologic, or histologic features have been identified that reliably predict which patients will achieve long-term remission with alpha interferon therapy. Several studies suggest that initiating interferon treatment early in the course of HCV infection is associated with a higher rate of resolved infection. The onset of HCV infection among healthcare workers (HCWs) after exposure can be detected earlier using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to identify HCV RNA, compared to enzyme immunoassay (EIA) for anti-HCV antibodies. However, PCR is not a licensed assay, and its accuracy is highly variable. There is no evidence to suggest that early treatment during chronic HCV infection is less effective than treatment initiated during the acute phase of infection. Furthermore, alpha interferon is only approved for the treatment of chronic hepatitis C. Neither IG nor antiviral agents are recommended for post-exposure prophylaxis of hepatitis C. Currently, no vaccine exists for hepatitis C. Healthcare institutions should consider implementing policies to monitor HCWs for HCV infection following percutaneous or mucosal exposure to blood. This monitoring may include serologic testing for anti-HCV antibodies and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity at baseline and six months post-exposure. All repeatedly reactive anti-HCV results by EIA should be confirmed with supplemental anti-HCV testing. HCWs should also be educated about the risks and prevention of occupational transmission of bloodborne pathogens, including hepatitis C, using accurate and up-to-date information. Occupational exposure generally does not increase HCWs' risk of hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection. When proper infection control practices are followed, nosocomial transmission of HAV is rare. However, outbreaks have occasionally been observed, such as transmission of HAV to neonatal intensive care unit staff by infants infected through transfused blood. Transmission of HAV from adult patients to HCWs is usually associated with fecal incontinence in the patients. Most patients hospitalized with hepatitis A are admitted after the onset of jaundice, when they are beyond the peak period of infectivity. Serologic surveys among various types of HCWs have not identified an elevated prevalence of HAV infection compared to other occupational populations. Two specific prophylactic measures are available for protection against hepatitis A: administration of immune globulin (IG) and the hepatitis A vaccine. When administered within two weeks of exposure, IG is more than 85% effective in preventing hepatitis A.
